scope: Targeted new comparisons of six rule accounts with assigned black-letter text; not a new independent opinion audit of every underlying case.

changes.old: A beneficiary is intended, and may enforce the promise, when recognising the right fits the parties' intention and the performance either pays the promisee's debt to the beneficiary or is meant as a gift to the beneficiary; every other beneficiary is incidental.
changes.new: A person outside the contract can enforce its promise when giving them that right fits the parties’ intent and the promised performance either pays a debt owed to them or was intended to benefit them. Merely benefiting by accident gives no such right. The contracting parties may agree otherwise.
changes.reason: Section 302(1)(b) is not limited to gifts; retain the opening agreement qualification.
changes.source: Contracts Selections PDF p.178, Restatement §302(1), comments c–d; ALI text via Lexis §302

changes.old: An agreement modifying a contract for the sale of goods needs no consideration to be binding; a signed clause may require modifications to be in a signed writing, a failed modification can still operate as a waiver, and a waiver of an executory term can be retracted on reasonable notice unless the other party has relied on it.
changes.new: For a sale of goods, parties can change their contract without exchanging new consideration, but good faith and applicable writing requirements still matter. An ineffective change may waive a requirement. A waiver covering future performance may be withdrawn with reasonable notice, unless that would unfairly harm someone who materially relied on it.
changes.reason: Retraction requires received reasonable notification and injustice from material reliance, not any reliance; good faith remains relevant.
changes.source: Contracts Selections PDF pp.344–345, UCC §2-209(1)–(5) and comment 2

changes.old:
Subsection (1) drops the pre-existing-duty rule for sales of goods: a modification needs no consideration. Subsection (2) lets a signed agreement exclude modification or rescission except by a signed writing, but a merchant's form imposing that requirement on a non-merchant must be separately signed by the other party. Subsection (3) keeps the statute of frauds in play if the contract as modified falls within it. Subsections (4) and (5) deal with waiver: an attempted modification that fails (2) or (3) can still operate as a waiver, and a waiver affecting an executory portion of the contract can be retracted by reasonable notification that strict performance will be required, unless retraction would be unjust because the other party has materially changed position in reliance on the waiver.

The section is the Code's answer to Alaska Packers' Association v. Domenico: instead of policing modifications by the consideration doctrine, the Code's comments test them for good faith. The Selections note that the 2003 Official Text of Article 1 covers the same point in § 1-303.
changes.new:
Subsection (1) drops the pre-existing-duty rule for sales of goods: a modification needs no consideration. Subsection (2) lets a signed agreement exclude modification or rescission except by a signed writing, but a merchant's form imposing that requirement on a non-merchant must be separately signed by the other party. Subsection (3) keeps the statute of frauds in play if the contract as modified falls within it. Subsections (4) and (5) deal with waiver: an attempted modification that fails (2) or (3) can still operate as a waiver, and a waiver affecting an executory portion of the contract can be retracted by reasonable notification that strict performance will be required, unless retraction would be unjust because the other party has materially changed position in reliance on the waiver.

The section is the Code's answer to Alaska Packers' Association v. Domenico: instead of policing modifications by the consideration doctrine, the Code's comments test them for good faith. Section 1-303(f) separately recognizes course of performance as evidence of waiver or modification, subject to § 2-209. The deletion footnote on the Selections page concerns the preceding § 2-208, not § 2-209.
changes.reason: A page footnote about §2-208 was incorrectly attributed to §2-209.
changes.source: Contracts Selections PDF p.344, footnote c after §2-208; §1-303(f), PDF p.321

changes.old: Course of performance, course of dealing and usage of trade are relevant to the meaning of the agreement and may explain or supplement even a final writing; where they cannot reasonably be reconciled with express terms, the express terms prevail, then course of performance, then course of dealing, then usage.
changes.new: Repeated performance, earlier dealings and trade practice can help explain or supplement a written sales agreement. Read them consistently with its express terms where reasonable. Otherwise, express terms generally come first, then performance, dealings and trade practice; a course of performance can also show waiver or modification.
changes.reason: The stated hierarchy is subject to §1-303(f), which permits course of performance to establish waiver/modification.
changes.source: Contracts Selections PDF pp.320–321, UCC §1-303(d)–(f); §2-202, PDF p.337

changes.old:
Section 1-303 (formerly § 1-205, with course of performance moved in from § 2-208) defines the three sources: a course of performance is repeated performance under the contract that the other side accepts without objection; a course of dealing is the parties' conduct in earlier transactions; a usage of trade is a practice observed so regularly in a place, vocation or trade that parties expect it to be observed, and its existence and scope are proved as facts. Subsection (d) makes all three relevant to the meaning of the agreement and lets them give particular meaning to, supplement or qualify its terms. Subsection (e) orders them when they cannot be reconciled: express terms first, then course of performance, course of dealing and usage of trade. Subsection (g) requires notice before a usage is used against a party, to prevent unfair surprise.

Section 2-202 applies this to the parol-evidence rule for sales of goods: terms in a writing intended as a final expression may not be contradicted by a prior agreement or a contemporaneous oral agreement, but may be explained or supplemented by course of performance, course of dealing or usage of trade, and by consistent additional terms unless the writing was intended as a complete and exclusive statement. Columbia Nitrogen, Nanakuli and Frigaliment show how far a usage can go in reading a written term.
changes.new:
Section 1-303 (formerly § 1-205, with course of performance moved in from § 2-208) defines the three sources: a course of performance is repeated performance under the contract that the other side accepts without objection; a course of dealing is the parties' conduct in earlier transactions; a usage of trade is a practice observed so regularly in a place, vocation or trade that parties expect it to be observed, and its existence and scope are proved as facts. Subsection (d) makes all three relevant to the meaning of the agreement and lets them give particular meaning to, supplement or qualify its terms. Subsection (e) orders them when they cannot be reconciled: express terms first, then course of performance, course of dealing and usage of trade. That hierarchy is subject to subsection (f): course of performance can show waiver or modification of an inconsistent term, subject to § 2-209. Subsection (g) requires notice before evidence of a usage is admitted against a party, to prevent unfair surprise.

Section 2-202 applies this to the parol-evidence rule for sales of goods: terms in a writing intended as a final expression may not be contradicted by a prior agreement or a contemporaneous oral agreement, but may be explained or supplemented by course of performance, course of dealing or usage of trade, and by consistent additional terms unless the writing was intended as a complete and exclusive statement. Columbia Nitrogen, Nanakuli and Frigaliment show how far a usage can go in reading a written term.
changes.reason: Preserve the express waiver exception to the hierarchy.

changes.old:
Subsection (1) states the test: specific performance may be decreed where the goods are unique 'or in other proper circumstances'. The second phrase loosens the traditional requirement that damages be inadequate, which is why the section marks a step in the specific-relief timeline. Subsection (2) lets the decree carry terms as to payment of the price, damages or other relief. Subsection (3) gives the buyer a right of replevin for goods identified to the contract when cover cannot be had after reasonable effort, or the goods were shipped under reservation and the security interest has been satisfied or tendered; for consumer goods the right vests when the buyer acquires a special property in the goods.

Morris v. Sparrow and the notes on personal-service contracts show the older equity limits that the section relaxes for sales of goods.
changes.new:
Subsection (1) states the test: specific performance may be decreed where the goods are unique 'or in other proper circumstances'. The second phrase allows relief beyond goods labelled unique; inability to obtain substitutes can show why damages are inadequate. It does not make specific performance automatic whenever a seller breaches. Subsection (2) lets the decree carry terms as to payment of the price, damages or other relief. Subsection (3) gives the buyer a right of replevin for goods identified to the contract when cover cannot be had after reasonable effort, circumstances indicate that effort would be unavailing, or the goods were shipped under reservation and the security interest has been satisfied or tendered; for consumer goods the right vests when the buyer acquires a special property in the goods.

Morris v. Sparrow and the notes on personal-service contracts show the older equity limits that the section relaxes for sales of goods.
changes.reason: Other proper circumstances expands beyond a uniqueness label, while equitable adequacy remains relevant; retain unavailing-cover alternative.
changes.source: Contracts Selections PDF pp.412–413, UCC §2-716(1), (3), comment 2

changes.old:
Section 205 is one sentence. It attaches the duty to every contract, and to two stages of it: performance and enforcement. It does not define good faith; the comments and the cases give the term its content case by case.

In this course the section is the Restatement's statement of the duty that Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon implied into an exclusive agency and that Bloor, Market Street Associates, Dalton and the later cases apply to discretion, efforts and the exercise of contractual powers. The UCC states the same obligation for sales in § 1-304 (formerly § 1-203).
changes.new:
Section 205 is one sentence. It attaches the duty to every contract, and to two stages of it: performance and enforcement. It does not define good faith; the comments and the cases give the term its content case by case.

In this course the section states the good-faith duty discussed in Bloor, Market Street Associates and Dalton. Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon is a related earlier decision implying a reasonable-efforts promise from an exclusive agency’s structure; it did not apply this later Restatement section, and implied efforts and good faith are distinct inquiries. The UCC states the same obligation for sales in § 1-304 (formerly § 1-203).
changes.reason: Wood implied a reasonable-efforts promise; avoid treating it as an application of the later good-faith section.
changes.source: Contracts Selections PDF p.110, Restatement §205; canonical Wood v. Lucy brief holding/reasoning
